1flcxyl: Spanish verbs are divided into three groups according to the infinitive: **-ar**, **-er**, and **-ir**. The biggest group is **-ar**: _trabajar, estudiar, hablar, enseñar, cocinar, escuchar, necesitar, viajar_.
6ylyhu: To conjugate a regular -ar verb, remove **-ar** (the stem is left: _trabaj-_) and add the ending for each person: **-o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an**. It's the same pattern you already use with _hablo, hablas, habla_ and with _me llamo, te llamas, se llama_.
16yrdmn: Since the ending already tells the person, the subject pronoun normally disappears: **Trabajo en un hospital** (there's no need for _yo_). Use the pronoun to contrast: **Yo** trabajo por la mañana y **ella** trabaja por la noche.
1ufjhs3: The present tense is used to talk about what you normally do (_Estudio por la tarde_) and also about what is true now in your life (_Trabajo en Monterrey_).
svacuy: Notice the strong syllable: **tra**-ba-jo, tra-**ba**-jas, tra-ba-**ja**-mos. In _trabajáis_ and _trabajás_ the stress goes at the end, which is why they take an accent mark.
7x5zup: _Trabajo_ is already the verb. You don't need _soy_ (in English you don't say «I am work» either).
4asexa: To say your profession use **ser + profession, with no article**: _Soy enfermera._ _Es ingeniero._ The article appears only if you add something more: Es **un** ingeniero muy bueno.
jithr5: Professions change gender like nationalities. In **-o → -a**: _médico, médica; abogado, abogada; ingeniero, ingeniera; enfermero, enfermera; cocinero, cocinera_. In **consonant → +a**: _profesor, profesora; programador, programadora; diseñador, diseñadora; contador, contadora_. In **-ista** and **-e** they are the same for both: _el/la periodista, el/la recepcionista, el/la estudiante, el/la gerente_.
1i7h4ac: For the place use **trabajar en + un / una / el / la + place**: _trabajo en un hospital, en una escuela, en la universidad, en una fábrica, en casa_ (without an article). To ask: **¿A qué te dedicas?**, **¿En qué trabajas?**, or **¿Qué estudias?** (with usted: _¿A qué se dedica?_).
13ehaj8: There is regional variation: in Mexico it's **mesero / mesera**; in Spain, **camarero / camarera**. In Mexico the accountant is **contador**; in Spain, **contable**.
tj2ln1: Profession ending in a consonant: add **-a** for the feminine.
1ykur5o: _Trabajar en casa_ (from your own home) goes without an article.
1qup4bs: Asking: qué, dónde, cuándo, cómo, quién, cuánto
1jnucmu: Question words **always take an accent mark**: **qué** (thing, information), **dónde** (place), **cuándo** (time), **cómo** (manner), **quién / quiénes** (person), **cuánto / cuánta / cuántos / cuántas** (quantity).
jw4cyl: The normal order is: **question word + verb + (subject)**: ¿Dónde trabaja **Ana**? ¿Qué estudian **tus amigos**? If there is a preposition, it goes in front of everything: **¿De dónde** eres? **¿En qué** trabajas? **¿Con quién** trabajas?
tgzlyg: **Cuánto** agrees with the noun like an adjective: _¿Cuántas horas trabajas?_ (horas, feminine plural), _¿Cuántos estudiantes hay?_ (masculine plural).
n6eipq: **Yes/no** questions need no question word and don't change the order: _Trabajas en Monterrey._ → _¿Trabajas en Monterrey?_ In writing, the signs **¿ ?** mark the difference; in speech, intonation does.
1o6t3ls: In the Caribbean (Cuba, Puerto Rico, Dominican Republic) it's normal to hear the subject before the verb: _¿Qué tú estudias?_ It's correct there; in most countries you say _¿Qué estudias (tú)?_
2940w0: Question words always take an accent mark.
1ntw2es: The question word goes at the beginning, and the question opens with **¿**.
pfnc7: From 21 to 29 it's written as **one word**: _veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés, veinticuatro, veinticinco, veintiséis, veintisiete, veintiocho, veintinueve_. _Veintidós, veintitrés_, and _veintiséis_ take an accent mark.
5o1b40: From 30 on, the tens and the units are **separate, joined with y**: _treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco, noventa y nueve_. The tens: **treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa**, and **cien**.
11n3isz: **Uno** changes before a noun: _veintiún estudiantes_, _treinta y un libros_ (masculine), _veintiuna personas_, _treinta y una sillas_ (feminine).
6nwjnd: **Cien** is exactly 100: _cien personas_. (From 101 you say _ciento uno_; you'll see that later.)
1fx52vn: In Monterrey phone numbers start with **81**: _ochenta y uno_. Many people say the number in pairs: _ochenta y uno, treinta y cuatro, cincuenta y cinco…_
1mnw485: **Y** adds two ideas: Soy ingeniera **y** trabajo en una fábrica. Remember: before the _i_ sound it becomes **e**: español **e** inglés.
137lmg1: **Pero** introduces an idea that contrasts or surprises: Soy médico, **pero** no trabajo en un hospital. Trabajo en una universidad.
1jqcny3: **También** adds something equal or of the same kind. It normally goes before the verb or at the end: **También** hablo inglés. / Hablo inglés **también**. To react to another person: —Trabajo en casa. —¡**Yo también**!
1832vg2: With a negative sentence, the reaction is **tampoco**: _—No trabajo los domingos. —Yo tampoco._ For now, just recognize it.

10xjcdf: In Spanish, a yes/no question has **the same words and the same order** as a statement: _Trabajas en Monterrey._ / _¿Trabajas en Monterrey?_ In writing, the signs **¿ ?** mark the question. In speech, only **intonation** marks it.
zji1cz: **Statement:** the voice falls at the end ↘. _Trabajas en Monterrey._ **Yes/no question:** the voice rises at the end ↗. _¿Trabajas en Monterrey?_ If you don't raise your voice, the other person hears a statement.
719c3x: **Question with qué, dónde, cuándo…:** the question word already says it's a question, so normally the voice **falls** at the end ↘: _¿Dónde trabajas?_ The question word is strong and a little higher. If you rise at the end, the question sounds friendlier or surprised.
1cui8vn: That's why **qué, dónde, cómo, cuándo, quién, cuánto** take an accent mark: in questions they are **stressed** (strong) words. Without an accent mark (_que, donde, como, cuando_) they are unstressed words that join sentences: Trabajo **donde** trabaja mi hermana.
j468d0: Variation: the melody changes a lot between countries. In the Caribbean many yes/no questions end falling; in Buenos Aires the voice rises and falls in a very marked way. But the basic rule, ↗ for yes/no and ↘ for statements, works throughout the Spanish-speaking world.
1tzqnc7: Questions are written with **¿** at the beginning and **?** at the end; exclamations with **¡ !**. If the question is only part of the sentence, the sign opens where the question begins: _Y tú, ¿dónde trabajas?_
zjmtqf: Say both versions in a row. First ↘, second ↗. The difference is only in the last strong syllable: _-rrey_.
